title: Learn by Doing: Performance, RISC and CISC
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then every past question on CPI, MIPS, Amdahl's law and RISC against CISC, each worked and then taught from nothing.
intro: Part A is the objective questions on this topic. Part B is past questions only, and two of these repeat across years: Amdahl's law with the same hypothetical cache, and RISC against CISC with example processors, which has been set in three separate papers.

lockin.big: "CPU time is instructions times CPI times clock period. Amdahl caps the speedup at 1 over the part you did not improve."
lockin.sub: MIPS is clock rate divided by CPI, divided by a million. RISC is fixed length, load and store, many registers; CISC is variable length, memory operands, microcode.

methodFrames.teach: One equation carries this topic: CPU time equals instruction count times cycles per instruction times the clock period. Every performance question is that equation with one term unknown.
methodFrames.ask: A program runs 1M instructions with an average CPI of 2.5 on a 500 MHz machine. How long does it take?

methodFrames.check: 1M times 2.5 times 2 ns, which is 5 ms.
methodFrames.teach: The clock period is 1 divided by the clock rate: 500 MHz gives 2 ns. Always convert the rate to a period before multiplying, and keep the units beside the numbers.
methodFrames.ask: Where does average CPI come from when a question gives you a mix of instruction types?

methodFrames.check: The weighted average: each type's share times its cycles, added up.
methodFrames.teach: So a mix of 40 per cent at 1 cycle, 20 per cent at 4 and 40 per cent at 2 gives 0.4 plus 0.8 plus 0.8, which is 2.0. Lay it out as a table with a share column and a product column, and the working earns its own marks.
methodFrames.ask: Now MIPS. From clock rate and CPI, what is the formula?

methodFrames.check: MIPS is the clock rate divided by CPI, divided by one million.
methodFrames.teach: And the warning worth a mark: MIPS compares two machines fairly only if they run the SAME program with the same instruction count, because a machine with a richer instruction set does more per instruction.
methodFrames.ask: Amdahl's law. A cache is ten times faster than memory and is used 90 per cent of the time. What limits the overall speedup?

methodFrames.check: The 10 per cent that was not speeded up.
methodFrames.teach: Amdahl: speedup equals 1 divided by ((1 minus f) plus f over k), where f is the fraction improved and k is how much faster that fraction became. Here 1 over (0.1 plus 0.09), which is about 5.3, not 10.
methodFrames.ask: State the law in one sentence, since 2 marks are usually for the statement alone.

methodFrames.check: The overall speedup is limited by the fraction of the work that cannot be improved.
methodFrames.teach: Write the sentence, then the formula, then the substitution. Three lines, three marks. Last piece, the comparison question: RISC is fixed length instructions, load and store only, many registers, hardwired control, one cycle per instruction; CISC is variable length, memory operands, fewer registers, microcoded, many cycles. Examples: ARM, MIPS, SPARC and PowerPC against Intel x86, Motorola 68000 and VAX.

exam.problem: Given 1,000,000 instructions ; per-mode share and cycles as tabled
exam.answer:
Find average CPI, total cycles, new CPI after optimising indirect, improvement
Formula CPI = Σ(fraction × cycles) · total = IC × CPI · improvement = (old − new)/old
Avg CPI = 0.40x1 + 0.20x1 + 0.15x2 + 0.10x4 + 0.10x3 + 0.05x2
        = 0.40 + 0.20 + 0.30 + 0.40 + 0.30 + 0.10
        = 1.70

Total cycles = 1,000,000 x 1.70 = 1,700,000

Indirect 4 -> 2:  new CPI = 1.70 - 0.10x4 + 0.10x2
                          = 1.70 - 0.20 = 1.50

Improvement = (1.70 - 1.50) / 1.70 = 0.20 / 1.70 = 11.76%
CPI 1.70; total cycles 1,700,000; new CPI 1.50; improvement 11.76%.

exam.problem: Given cache 10 times faster than memory ; used 85% of the time
exam.answer:
Find state Amdahl's law, then the overall speedup
Formula S = 1 / ((1−f) + f/s), with f the sped-up fraction and s its speedup

Amdahl's law states that the overall speedup obtainable by improving one part of a system is limited by the fraction of the total time that part is actually used: even if that part is made infinitely fast, the speedup can never exceed 1/(1−f), where f is the fraction of the time that is sped up.

f = 0.85 (cache hits), s = 10
S = 1 / ((1 - 0.85) + 0.85/10)
  = 1 / (0.15 + 0.085)
  = 1 / 0.235
  = 4.26
S = 4.26, far below 10, because the 15% of slow accesses dominate.

exam.problem: Cover the answer and work this yourself first, from the question and method set out just above. Then reveal and check line by line.
exam.answer:
Break it downbefore you compute
Given four architecture names and nothing numeric.
Asked compare two architectures with diagrams, then mention four differences and give four example processors. Three verbs, and the diagrams are compulsory, not decoration.
Marks 3 + 4 = 7. In part (ii) that is four differences plus four processors for 4 marks, so half a mark a line: write in a two column table, not prose.
Taught in Module One Unit 1 for the architectures, Module Four Unit 1 for RISC and CISC.
Trap forgetting the diagrams. They are explicitly asked for and carry their own marks, and a compare answered as prose alone cannot score full marks however good the prose is. The second trap is naming processors nobody can check: ARM and MIPS against x86 and 68000 are safe.
(i) Von Neumann uses one memory and one bus for instructions and data, so it is simpler and cheaper but the shared bus carries only one at a time. Harvard uses separate memories and buses, so an instruction fetch and a data access happen simultaneously: faster, but more hardware and less flexible. Draw both diagrams; they carry marks of their own.

questions.heading: 2023/2024, Q1(b)

scenario.text: b. i) State Amdahl's law' 2½mks ii) Assume in hypothetical system cache is 10 times faster than main memory and CPU accesses the cache 85% of the time. Using Amdahl's law, calculate the overall speed up of the system. 2mks

questions.asked: This question repeats. The same question, amdahl’s law, was also set in 2025/2026 Q3(c). Wording and numbers move; the method does not.

breakdown.question: What is this question actually asking, what have you been given, and what do the marks tell you about how much to write? Decide, then check.
breakdown.answer:
Given a cache 10 times faster than main memory, and a CPU that finds what it needs in the cache 85% of the time.

Asked two things. First "State" the law, which is a statement in words plus the formula, not the formula alone. Then "calculate the overall speed up of the system".

Marks 2mks (2½mks in 23/24) for the statement and 2mks for the number, so the words are worth as much as the arithmetic. Write the law out.

Taught in this unit, the Must memorise box directly above.

Trap reading "10 times faster" as the answer. That is s, and it applies only to the fraction f = 0.85. The 15% still going to main memory at full cost is what holds the whole machine down to about 4.26.

exam.problem: Answer 2023/2024 Q1(b) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Given f = 0.85 (the 85% of accesses served by cache) · s = 10 (cache is ten times faster than main memory)
Find the overall speedup of the machine
Formula speedup = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s)
what each symbol means f = the fraction of the work the improvement touches, here the cache hits · s = how many times faster that fraction runs · (1 − f) = the 15% still going to main memory at full cost, which is what caps the answer well below 10
  1. The sped-up fraction is f = 0.85 (the cache accesses), and the speedup factor is s = 10.
  2. Speedup = 1 / ((1 − 0.85) + 0.85 / 10) = 1 / (0.15 + 0.085).
  3. = 1 / 0.235 = 4.26.
Speedup = 1 / (0.15 + 0.085) = 1 / 0.235 ≈ 4.26 times.

Now redo it: notice the answer is far below 10, because the 15% of slow accesses dominate. That is exactly the point Amdahl's law makes.

Asked a fixed number of "clear differences", then two example processors of each family. Both halves are marked and the examples are the half students forget.

Taught in this unit, the comparison table directly above.

exam.problem: Answer 2023/2024 Q5(c) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Four differences (any four): RISC has few simple fixed-length one-cycle instructions and only load/store touch memory, with many registers and simple pipelined hardware; CISC has many complex variable-length multi-cycle instructions, many of which access memory directly, with fewer registers and complex hardware. Examples: RISC, ARM and MIPS (also SPARC, PowerPC); CISC, Intel x86 (8086, Pentium) and the Motorola 68000.

Now redo it: pick your four contrasts (instruction count, length, cycles, memory access) and memorise two examples each: ARM/MIPS for RISC, x86/68000 for CISC.

exam.problem: Answer 2020/2021 Q4(b) in full in your book, then open this and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Four clear differences between RISC and CISC.

RISCCISC
Instruction setSmall and simple, each instruction doing one thingLarge and complex, single instructions doing multi step work
Instruction lengthFIXED length, which makes decoding and pipelining simpleVARIABLE length, so decoding is harder and pipelining awkward
Memory accessLOAD and STORE only: arithmetic works on registersInstructions may operate directly on memory operands
Control unitHardwired, and typically one instruction per cycleMicrocoded, and many cycles per instruction
RegistersMany general purpose registersFewer registers, with more addressing modes instead
Where the work goesInto the compiler, which emits more instructionsInto the hardware, which does more per instruction

Two example processors in each category.

  • RISC: ARM and MIPS. SPARC and PowerPC also earn the mark.
  • CISC: the Intel x86 family and the Motorola 68000. The DEC VAX also earns it.

Convergence: modern x86 processors decode their complex instructions into simple internal operations, so the difference now lives in the instruction set the programmer sees rather than in how the chip is built.
